metadata.tags: Upbeat early-2000s French house and futuristic disco, around 118–122 BPM. Punchy four-on-the-floor drums, warm funky bass, filtered disco loops, bright analog synth chords, shimmering arpeggios, rhythmic guitar fragments, and sweeping filter builds. Male robotic/vocoder lead vocal with heavy autotune, emotionally warm despite the synthetic delivery. Verses should be simple and reflective; chorus becomes huge, euphoric, repetitive, and instantly catchy around “Again / Differently.” Use chopped vocal samples, call-and-response robot voices, brief breakdowns, and long instrumental grooves. Gradually introduce subtle musical changes each time sections repeat, reinforcing the idea that nothing returns exactly the same. Nostalgic, joyful, thoughtful, futuristic, danceable, and slightly bittersweet. Around 4 minutes.

metadata.tags: High-energy old-school East Coast alternative hip-hop with a gritty Brooklyn feel, fused with electro, techno, funk, punk energy, and sample-heavy production. Three distinct male rappers rapidly trade lines, interrupt each other, shout responses, and finish each other’s phrases with playful comic timing. Crunchy breakbeats, distorted bass, turntable scratches, drum-machine loops, funky guitar stabs, analog synth bleeps, robotic vocoder voices, glitch effects, chopped samples, and abrupt stop-start transitions. Fast, sarcastic, witty, chaotic, and slightly absurd rather than aggressive. Verses should feel loose and conversational; hooks should be big group shouts. A robotic voice confidently interrupts throughout and gradually becomes less certain. Raw, energetic, weird, clever, and unpredictable.

metadata.tags: Early-1970s British psychedelic art-pop pushed further into kaleidoscopic experimentation, still in three distinct connected sections with contrasting tunes, rhythms and chord progressions, joined by trippy instrumental bridges. Warm, roomy live drums with splashing cymbals, highly melodic, wandering bass lines, chiming acoustic guitar, fuzz-drenched electric guitar, and dry, close-mic’d piano that drops in as a surreal accent. Expanded psychedelic textures: tape-saturated delays, reverse swells, varispeed moments, gentle phasing and flanging on guitars and backing vocals, and occasional warped room ambience. Strings, oboe, English horn and French horn appear as unexpected, echo-like colors and drifting countermelodies, treated with mild tape wow and pitch bends so they feel otherworldly rather than orchestral. Part I stays intimate, pastoral and slightly uncanny; Part II dissolves into a dreamier, more lysergic soundscape with swirling vocal harmonies and hazy, reverb-washed bridges;

[Part I — A Very Pleasant Morning]

We left the house at half past nine
The hedges smelled of rain,
Mrs. Bell was sweeping leaves,
The porter waved his cane.

Gerald wore his Sunday coat,
Mabel brought the tea,
Arthur said, “The road bends left,”
And everyone agreed.

The church bell rang at ten to ten,
A blackbird crossed the lane,
Everything was where it ought to be—

Until Gerald moved the sign.

[Bridge]

Only six or seven feet.
A perfectly sensible distance.

The sign said LEFT.
The road went right.

So naturally—

We followed the sign.

[Part II — Somewhere After Somewhere]

We passed a house with thirteen doors
And windows painted green.
A gentleman was selling clocks
That all read seventeen.

The postman sailed across a field
Inside a paper boat.
A lady asked us where we’d been.
We said, “We rather hoped you’d know.”

The road grew narrow, then grew wide,
Then climbed into a tree.
Arthur said, “According to the rules,
This shouldn’t trouble me.”

Nobody could have known.
Nobody could have guessed.
The moon came out at half past noon
And buttoned up its vest.

We met the mayor upside down.
He shook us by the shoe.

“Are we still heading west?” asked Mabel.

“West of what?” he said.

[Bridge]

The sign had grown enormously.

Or perhaps
we had become very small.

Gerald said there was no cause for alarm.

And somewhere in the distance,

the sea began to ring.

[Part III — A Perfectly Reasonable Disaster]

It was a perfectly reasonable disaster,
Every little piece made sense.
The river climbed the chimney
And the garden cleared the fence.

The houses floated upside down,
The stars came out in rows,
And everyone kept nodding
As if everyone supposed—

This was a perfectly reasonable disaster,
Nothing stranger than before.
There were fishes in the treetops,
There were keyholes without doors.

The king arrived by bicycle.
The clouds began to sing.
Gerald tipped his hat and said,
“Well, that explains everything.”

No villain in the tower.
No dragon in the rain.
Just one small sign moved sideways
And the world forgot its name.

Every choice was sensible.
Every choice sincere.

Funny how a reasonable road
Can leave you nowhere near.

Then morning came.

The hedges smelled of rain.

Mrs. Bell was sweeping leaves.

The porter waved his cane.

And Gerald found the signpost
Standing quietly by the lane.

He looked at us.

We looked at him.

He turned it round again.

[Pause]

“Better.”

metadata.tags: 3–4 minute theatrical space rap battle between two distinct male voices: “Certainty” is confident, booming, fast, declarative; “Question” is nimble, amused, conversational, and rhythmically unpredictable. Old-school hip-hop battle energy fused with futuristic electro, space-funk, glitch, vocoder, analog synths, deep bass, crisp drums, and mission-control samples. Hard beat cuts every time someone says “Wait, what?” Use call-and-response, interruptions, overlapping bars, short spoken exchanges, and escalating verbal sparring. Keep it clever, funny, skeptical, and musically serious—not campy. Bridge becomes increasingly glitchy and recursive before snapping back into a huge final hook. End with quiet mission-control dialogue: “Trajectory recalculated.” “So we’re good?” “…probably.”

metadata.tags: Early-1970s psychedelic soul and funk with a warm, slightly gritty analog sound. Deep melodic bass, dry pocket drums, wah-wah electric guitar, clavinet, Rhodes electric piano, subtle organ, hand percussion, and occasional lush strings or horn accents. Relaxed mid-tempo groove with lots of space, syncopation, and live-band looseness. Soulful male lead vocal, conversational and slightly raspy, moving between low intimate verses and light falsetto touches. Playful call-and-response backing vocals in the breakdown. The chorus should feel instantly memorable but understated, built around “The truth got a side door.” Philosophical, sly, earthy, and human rather than preachy. Vintage tape warmth, small imperfections, extended instrumental fills, and a gently psychedelic atmosphere. Avoid disco gloss, modern pop production, aggressive funk, or oversized vocal theatrics.

metadata.tags: Bright, joyful African choral anthem with a large mixed choir, powerful call-and-response vocals, layered harmonies, handclaps, stomps, ululation, and energetic traditional percussion. Sung primarily in Swahili, with expressive solo voices answered by the full ensemble. Fast, buoyant rhythm with warm hand drums, shakers, bells, marimba-like melodic percussion, subtle bass, and occasional brass or flute accents. Cinematic and theatrical but organic, communal, playful, and deeply uplifting. Build from a simple solo opening into increasingly huge choir sections, with a lively percussion dance break and an explosive final chorus around “BADO TUNAENDA!” and “INATOSHA!” Keep the melodies simple, memorable, and easy for a crowd to sing. Avoid electronic dance production, pop-rock guitars, or solemn gospel; this should feel sunlit, rhythmic, celebratory, and alive.
